facts.text: Scalar-output agreement compares a single simulation result with the same physical-test result, such as stopping distance or braking-trigger time, usually as a percentage error with an agreed error band.
facts.quote: Scalar-output agreement compares one number from the simulation with the same number from the physical test, for example stopping distance or the time at which braking was triggered, usually as a percentage error with an agreed error band.

facts.text: The simplest scalar-output agreement check calculates relative error as the absolute difference between simulated and measured values divided by the measured value.
The booklet's aircraft-seat certification example compares a measured load peak of 1,315 lb with a simulated peak of 1,360 lb, giving a relative error of 3.42%.
facts.quote: A measured load peak of 1,315 lb and a simulated peak of 1,360 lb give (1360 minus 1315) divided by 1315, that is 3.42%.

facts.text: The aviation guidance in the booklet's aircraft-seat certification example uses 10% criteria for several quantities, agreed in advance.
facts.quote: The aviation guidance uses 10% criteria for several quantities, agreed in advance [Chapter 10].

facts.text: An illustrative braking comparison of a measured stopping distance of 38.0 m and a simulated stopping distance of 39.5 m gives an error of 3.9%.
facts.quote: For braking the equivalent might be: measured stopping distance 38.0 m, simulated 39.5 m, error 3.9%.

facts.text: Scalar-output agreement error bands must account for uncertainty because uncertainty consumes part of the margin to a limit.
facts.quote: An error band must respect uncertainty.

facts.text: In the aircraft-seat certification example, the regulatory maximum load is 1,500 lb and physical-test scatter is about 42 lb standard deviation.
facts.quote: the regulatory maximum is 1,500 lb and the test scatter about 42 lb standard deviation

facts.text: In the aircraft-seat certification example, achieving 95% confidence that the true load remains below the 1,500 lb limit requires a prediction below about 1,431 lb, calculated as 1,500 minus 1.645 times the 42 lb standard deviation.
facts.quote: for 95% confidence that the true value stays below the limit, the prediction must stay below about 1,431 lb (1500 minus 1.645 times 42).

facts.text: A predicted load of 1,490 lb is insufficient in the aircraft-seat certification example despite being below the 1,500 lb regulatory maximum, because uncertainty consumes part of the margin.
facts.quote: Predicting 1,490 lb is not enough just because it is below 1,500: uncertainty consumes part of the margin [Chapter 10].

facts.text: Scalar-output agreement is necessary but insufficient for automatic-braking validation: two systems can reach the same peak deceleration at different times, changing whether a collision occurs.
facts.quote: Scalars are necessary but not sufficient. Two systems can reach the same peak deceleration at very different times, and for automatic braking that changes whether the collision happens [Chapter 10].

facts.text: The booklet recommends stopping-distance error, intervention-time error, residual impact-speed error, range error and relative-speed error as scalar quantities for the heavy off-road automatic-braking validation program.
facts.quote: The booklet recommends scalar quantities for this program, including stopping-distance error, intervention-time error, residual impact-speed error and range and relative-speed errors

facts.text: The booklet warns against copying the aviation 10% agreement criterion as a generic tolerance for off-road braking.
facts.quote: warns that the aviation 10% figure must not be copied as a generic tolerance for off-road braking [Chapter 10].
